scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

message.reasoning:
The scenario describes a situation where the couple, who are non-religious, agreed to include religious elements in their wedding ceremony to accommodate the religious preferences of the bride's parents, who were paying for the wedding. However, the officiant did not include those religious aspects, leading to the parents feeling "spiritually assaulted" and making demands for a subsequent religious blessing. The couple feels upset by the parents' reaction and their conditional gift, and they are considering compromising by having a blessing recorded locally and sent to the parents, or refusing the gift and limiting contact.

The question is whether the couple's actions (or proposed actions) are morally acceptable. The core issue is whether it is morally acceptable for the couple to have a non-religious wedding ceremony despite having agreed to include religious elements, and then to respond to the parents' demands as they plan.

Key points:
- The couple is atheist/agnostic and did not want a religious ceremony.
- They agreed to include religious elements to appease the parents, who were paying.
- The officiant failed to include those elements, which was not the couple's intention.
- The parents reacted strongly, feeling spiritually assaulted, and made demands.
- The couple feels wronged by the parents' lack of benefit of the doubt and conditional gift.
- They are considering a compromise (recording a blessing) or refusing the gift.

The moral evaluation should focus on the couple's actions: having a non-religious ceremony (which was accidental due to the officiant's failure) and their response to the parents' demands.

Is it morally acceptable for the couple to have a non-religious ceremony? They initially agreed to include religious elements to respect the parents' wishes, but the officiant did not follow through. The couple did not intentionally deceive or disrespect the parents; it was an accident. Therefore, their action (having a non-religious ceremony) was not morally wrong because it was not deliberate.

Is it morally acceptable for the couple to refuse the parents' conditional gift and limit contact? The parents are imposing conditions on a gift (the money they gave) and making demands that the couple finds unreasonable. The couple has the right to set boundaries and refuse conditional gifts. It is not morally wrong to decline a gift that comes with strings attached, especially when the conditions are seen as disrespectful or coercive.

Additionally, the couple is considering a compromise by having a blessing recorded locally. This shows an attempt to respect the parents' feelings while maintaining their own boundaries. This compromise is a morally acceptable way to handle the situation, as it seeks a middle ground without fully yielding to unreasonable demands.

Overall, the couple's actions—having an accidentally non-religious ceremony and responding to the parents' demands with a compromise or refusal—are morally acceptable. They are not intentionally causing harm, and they are standing up for their autonomy in a reasonable manner.

Therefore, the answer should be 1 (morally acceptable).
